quantity.description: Change in own-team expected single-game scoring margin from adopting the strategy
quantity.support: unbounded real; positive favors own team

prior.consistency_check: Most plausible value 0.45 lies inside [-0.1, 1.35]; skew-normal support is all reals, so signed effects are covered. Fit is approximate (mode off by ~0.02).

distribution_family.justification: The downside is bounded by execution slippage (the model floor is roughly break-even by construction), while the upside from compounding good decisions and forcing opponent counter-adjustments is longer, so the interval is asymmetric around the mode.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fit numerically: with alpha=2.4 (delta≈0.92), the standardized SN mode is ≈0.66 and its central 95% quantiles are ≈[-0.25, 2.15]; scaling gives mode ≈ 0.02 + 0.62×0.66 ≈ 0.43 (target 0.45) and 95% mass ≈ [0.02 − 0.16, 0.02 + 1.33] ≈ [-0.13, 1.35], matching targets to within rounding.

strategies.rationale: Public EPA/WP research consistently shows league-wide punting and kicking rates well below model-optimal thresholds; capturing that gap converts free expected points into wins over a season, and my only objective is wins, not media insulation.
strategies.recommendation: Go for it on 4th down whenever a win-probability model says it is at least break-even, including 4th-and-short from midfield and inside our own 40 in neutral game states, and take the modeled 2-point conversion in trailing score states (e.g., down 8) rather than defaulting to the kick.
strategies.title: Model-Calibrated 4th-Down Aggressiveness

prior.consistency_check: 0.35 lies inside [-0.4, 1.1] and is the interval midpoint; normal support is all reals, covering signed effects.

distribution_family.justification: My interval is symmetric about the most plausible value and I see no mechanism for extreme outcomes in either direction — defenses adapt, capping upside, while the floor is a modest efficiency loss from predictability.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Published EPA-per-play analyses show early-down passes, especially play-action, outperform runs in neutral situations, and that play-action efficacy does not require 'establishing the run'; league play-calling still lags this, leaving expected points on the table each game.
strategies.recommendation: Raise 1st/2nd-down dropback rate in neutral game states toward the top of the league, with heavy use of play-action on early downs regardless of prior run success.
strategies.title: Early-Down Pass Rate and Play-Action Expansion

prior.consistency_check: 0.2 lies inside [-0.5, 0.9] at the midpoint; normal support is all reals, covering signed effects.

distribution_family.justification: The public evidence here is directional but weaker than for 4th downs, and offenses can counter with heavier run rates; I expect a small centered effect with roughly symmetric adjustment risk on both sides.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: EPA research shows explosive passes drive scoring far more than incremental run yardage; trading a fraction of a yard per carry against the run for fewer deep completions is a positive-expectation swap that most defenses still under-execute out of run-fit pride.
strategies.recommendation: Default to two-high safety shells with light boxes in neutral situations, conceding modest run efficiency to suppress explosive passes, and blitz below league average since pressure-rate gains rarely justify coverage exposure.
strategies.title: Light Boxes and Two-High Structural Default

prior.consistency_check: 0.1 lies inside [-0.55, 0.75]; Student-t support is all reals, covering signed effects.

distribution_family.justification: I genuinely don't know the trade-off rate between saved snaps and lost clock assets; a symmetric center near zero with heavy tails reflects a real chance I'm meaningfully wrong in either direction.
distribution_family.name: student_t

parameters.conversion_note: nu = 7 for moderately heavy tails (t_{0.975,7} ≈ 2.36); mu = 0.1; sigma = (0.75 − (−0.55)) / (2 × 2.36) = 1.3 / 4.72 ≈ 0.275 (scale parameter, not SD).

strategies.rationale: One clean, correctly-matched defensive snap at a hinge moment can be worth more than a marginal end-of-half clock asset; public analytics prices timeouts mainly via end-of-game clock models and is essentially silent on their value as call-correction insurance mid-drive, so this rests on my judgment about how often a compromised call costs a conversion.
strategies.recommendation: Spend a timeout before the snap on the opponent's highest-leverage 3rd/4th downs (e.g., 3rd-and-3 in the red zone) whenever our call is compromised — wrong personnel, tipped disguise, or a bad matchup — rather than hoarding timeouts for end-of-half offense.
strategies.title: Pre-Snap Defensive Timeouts at Peak Leverage

prior.consistency_check: 0.15 lies inside [-0.7, 1.2]; skew-normal support is all reals, covering signed effects. Fit is approximate (mode off by ~0.01).

distribution_family.justification: Downside is capped near the cost of some rushed, lower-quality calls and occasional own-defense fatigue, while the upside — regularly converting one explosive into two — has a longer tail, so the interval is asymmetric.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fit numerically: with alpha=1.3, the standardized SN mode is ≈0.46 and central 95% quantiles ≈[-1.20, 2.40]; scaling gives mode ≈ −0.08 + 0.52×0.46 ≈ 0.16 (target 0.15) and 95% mass ≈ [−0.08 − 0.62, −0.08 + 1.25] ≈ [-0.70, 1.17], matching targets to within rounding.

strategies.rationale: My experience is that defenses are most structurally broken in the 20 seconds after a chunk play — busted rotations and wrong personnel stuck on the field — and stacking a second strike there compounds drives; public analytics on tempo is mixed and doesn't isolate this specific post-explosive window, so this is coaching judgment, not model consensus.
strategies.recommendation: After any gain of 15+ yards, sprint to the line and snap a pre-scripted shot or constraint play within ~12 seconds, attacking before the defense can substitute, align, or communicate the next call.
strategies.title: Explosive-Play Sprint Tempo Package

prior.consistency_check: 0.05 lies inside [-0.9, 1.0]; Student-t support is all reals, covering signed effects. Interval is treated as symmetric about mu to within 0.02 of the stated bounds.

distribution_family.justification: This is a genuinely untested scheme choice: it could be a nothing-burger, a meaningful edge, or a self-inflicted wound via blown fits, so I want a symmetric center near zero with heavy tails in both directions.
distribution_family.name: student_t

parameters.conversion_note: nu = 4 for clearly heavy tails (t_{0.975,4} ≈ 2.78); mu = 0.05; sigma = (1.0 − (−0.9)) / (2 × 2.78) = 1.9 / 5.56 ≈ 0.342 (scale parameter, not SD).

strategies.rationale: Pre-snap protection identification is the quarterback's cheapest advantage, and denying it should degrade protection calls and hot reads at the exact moments that decide drives; public analytics has essentially nothing on amoeba-specific effects, and I concede this is a judgment call with real bust risk from my own alignment errors — honestly, the most plausible net effect is close to zero.
strategies.recommendation: On 3rd-and-7+, deploy a no-hand-in-the-ground 'amoeba' front with all seven front players standing and roaming until the snap, randomizing rushers between 3 and 6 from game to game.
strategies.title: Amoeba Front on Obvious Passing Downs
